Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] In historic judgment, ICJ concludes that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims
item.description:
In historic judgment, ICJ concludes that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims

Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 08:16
The UN's top court holds a state responsible for genocide in a historic precedent that will help shape the decision in South Africa's case against Israel
The International Criminal Court in The Hague pictured on 28 March (AFP)
Off

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague on Thursday concluded that Myanmar’s security forces committed genocide during the brutal 2017 “clearance operations” against its Muslim Rohingya minority.

The court said genocidal intent was “the only reasonable inference” that could be drawn from the evidence of Myanmar's conduct taken as a whole and that Mynamar intended to destroy a substantial part of the protected group. 

The court found that the Rohingya are a protected ethnic group under Article II of the Genocide Convention. It also held that the conduct of Myanmar’s security forces was attributable to the state."

"The court is fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts under Acts 2 (a) (b) and (d) with the intent to desroy substantial parts of the Rohingya," the ICJ held.

The court said the three genocidal acts committed by the Myanmar are killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, and imposing conditions intended to prevent births within the group. 

It found that Myanmar’s security forces carried out indiscriminate killings, committed sexual violence, including against children, and attacked Rohingya as they fled.

The court said security forces burned Rohingya homes and that villages were systematically destroyed. In some areas, permanent infrastructure was built and non-Rohingya residents were resettled on the land.

The judges acknowledged attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) and said witness accounts of those attacks were consistent with other evidence before the court. They also traced how the rights of the Rohingya, who had lived in Myanmar for generations, had been progressively eroded and how military-sponsored hate speech had fuelled hostility against them.

The court said The Gambia bore the burden of identifying and proving the facts supporting its claims. It acknowledged that the rule can be applied flexibly in some circumstances.

In assessing the evidence, the judges took into account Myanmar’s failure to investigate the alleged atrocities and to provide access to victims and witnesses.

The judges said allegations of genocide require “fully conclusive” evidence, while claims that a state failed to prevent or punish genocide require a high level of certainty.

In its earlier genocide cases concerning Bosnia and Croatia, the court could draw on findings by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. 

In this case, it said it had no comparable judicial findings to draw on and had to make its own assessment of the evidence submitted by the parties.

The court heard from witnesses who had directly experienced the violence. It said key statements went unchallenged and that witnesses’ descriptions were consistent with other evidence. It gave weight to second-hand accounts where they were corroborated.

Myanmar did not allow either the UN fact-finding mission or the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) to enter the country.

The judges treated the fact-finding mission’s reports with caution because it used a lower standard of proof than the court. They nevertheless considered the reports reliable sources of factual evidence, noting that the mission had carried out substantial fieldwork in Bangladesh.

The court gave considerable weight to statements collected by the IIMM, citing its careful methodology. It also considered material from the rights group Legal Action Worldwide generally reliable, while giving it less evidentiary weight.

The judges said genocidal intent “may exist alongside other purposes”, but they found that Myanmar’s stated aim of combating the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) did not reasonably explain the pattern of attacks.

They also rejected forcible displacement as an alternative explanation, pointing to evidence that security forces killed Rohingya as they fled towards Bangladesh.

Historic precedent

The court's ruling marks the first time the United Nations' top court has held a state fully responsible for committing genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The case was filed by the Gambia on 11 November 2019 at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). 

It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court. 

It is also the first judgment in a case with large-scale intervention by third states.

Eleven states have intervened, filing submissions on how the Genocide Convention should be interpreted, but mainly in support of the Gambia's case rather than as parties. The states, also present at the court on Thursday, are: Belgium, Canada, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Denmark, France, Germany, the Republic of Ireland, the Maldives, the Netherlands, Slovenia and the United Kingdom.

The ruling is final and binding, with no right of appeal.

Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.

Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.

The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
Read More »

The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes. 

About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement.

Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel.

The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention during its campaign against the Rohingya from 25 August 2017. 

The operations were carried out under Min Aung Hlaing, then the military's commander-in-chief. 

Myanmar at the time had a civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, but the military-drafted constitution left the armed forces outside its control.

In February 2021, Min Aung Hlaing overthrew Suu Kyi's government in a coup, and in April this year he stepped down as army chief.

He was later elected president by a parliament dominated by military-backed lawmakers, following elections organised by the junta.

Rohingya fled mass killings, rape and the burning of villages during what the military described as "clearance operations".

The case is a dispute between states, so the court will decide whether Myanmar as a state is responsible, not whether any individual is guilty. 

A finding against Myanmar would arguably add to international pressure on Min Aung Hlaing, whose move to the presidency is widely perceived as a bid for international legitimacy.

In 2018, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that there was sufficient information to infer genocidal intent and recommended that senior military officials be investigated and prosecuted for genocide.

On 11 November 2019, the Gambia filed its case at the ICJ with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). 

It was the first time a state not directly affected had brought a genocide case before the court. 

The west African country relied on the principle that every state party to the 1948 Genocide Convention has a common interest in seeing it upheld.

In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, then Myanmar's civilian leader, appeared at the court to deny the allegations. 

In January 2020, after finding "a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice to the rights" of the Rohingya under the Genocide Convention, the court ordered Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence.

The court rejected Myanmar's objections to its jurisdiction in July 2022, and heard the merits of the case from 12-29 January 2026, including closed-door testimony from Rohingya witnesses.

This is a developing story.

Assessment of damage is underway, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia

The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, leading to a halt in train services, two days after a dramatic Ukrainian air raid had knocked out the road bridge alongside.

Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] New law ‘may be needed’ after Google rejects call to remove Russell Brand’s YouTube prison message
item.description:
Ex-minister Jess Phillips admits government does not have power to compel platforms to remove distressing content

  • UK politics live – latest updates

A new online safety act is likely to be needed to tackle convicted criminals such as Russell Brand using social media platforms to broadcast messages from prison, Labour MP Jess Phillips has said.

Just days after his conviction, Brand’s wife, Laura, broadcast a message from her husband to their 6.6 million YouTube subscribers, claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences for which he had been convicted by a jury. The video has had almost 850,000 views.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Cousin fights cousin as war in Yemen splits families down the middle
item.description:
Cousin fights cousin as war in Yemen splits families down the middle

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Wed, 11/18/2026 - 15:27
Communities fracture with loyalties split between the Houthis and the internationally recognised government
A fighter loyal to Yemen's government on the front line around Mount al-Midan in Taiz province, on 26 October 2026 (Ahmad al-Basha/AFP)
Off

It wasn’t easy for Mukhtar, 45, to flee his home in the village where he was born and raised, 50 kilometres south of Taiz city. However, he felt forced to leave in 2019, believing that the Houthis (also known as Ansar Allah) were fighting for a noble cause in Yemen and that he needed to support them.

Mukhtar had been living in an area controlled by the Saudi Arabia-backed government, and the prospect of staying there any longer had become dangerous. Many of his relatives, including his brothers and cousins, supported government forces, and he feared he might be detained, like so many others.

“Many Ansar Allah supporters were detained or fled their villages; not just fighters, but civilians and sheikhs who supported them. So there was no choice but to flee my village and live in Ansar Allah-controlled areas,” Mukhtar told Middle East Eye.

Back in his village, Mukhtar had worked as a farmer and part-time land broker, but he lost his livelihood when he fled. When he reached a Houthi area, he joined the group, convinced that they were driven not by money but by a desire to defend Islam.

“Ansar Allah’s project is for the hereafter; they implement what is in the Quran rather than following the orders of foreign countries. Theirs is a project for the afterworld, not a project of mercenaries,” Mukhtar added.

On 3 September, Houthi forces launched a heavy offensive against government troops in southern Hodeidah and the western district of Taiz, seizing large areas of both governorates.

On 4 October they launched another major attack, capturing the remaining areas of Taiz that had been outside their control, leaving only Taiz city and parts of Jabal Sabir in the hands of government forces.

Mukhtar took part in these battles gladly, seeing them as a chance to finally return home after seven years of displacement.

'One of [war's] ugliest faces is seeing brothers and cousins fight each other'

– Abdulrahman, 64, an uncle of warring cousins

“Ultimately, it is Allah who granted us victory because of the justice of our cause, and whoever stands with Allah, He will never forsake,” he said.

Mukhtar is now back in his village. However, as soon as he arrived alongside Houthi forces, his cousin Mohammed fled. As a fighter with the government forces, Mohammed feared that if he stayed, Mukhtar would not leave him to live in peace.

Mukhtar insists he would not harm him, pointing to a "general amnesty" declared by the Houthi leadership for those who lay down their arms and return home.

The Houthis and pro-government forces backed by the Saudi Arabia-led coalition have been fighting in Yemen since 2015, but over the past two months Houthi forces have made dramatic advances and are now around 60km from Aden, Yemen’s temporary capital.

While some government fighters have stopped fighting and returned to civilian life, many others, like Mohammed, continue to fight alongside government forces in Lahj governorate. 

'We must accept different beliefs'

Mohammed, 37, who spoke to MEE by phone, opposes the Houthis and believes they have come to alter the religious "doctrine" of the people in his area, accusing local fighters like his cousin of being "traitors".

“It is true that the Houthi militia took over large areas in a few days, but that was only because of the traitors who helped them do it,” he told MEE.

“We are still fighting, and what was lost in a few days will be taken back in a few days, and all traitors will meet their proper punishment.”

As soon as the Houthis enter an area, not only fighters but many other opponents flee towards government-held areas, fearing they will be arrested if they remain under Houthi control.

When asked about fighting his own cousin, Mohammed replied: “He isn’t a cousin any more, since he stood with the militias against his family.

“We were in our homes and didn’t exile anyone; those who supported the Houthis fled on their own to fight alongside them, not because we forced them out,” he added.

'We were in our homes and didn’t exile anyone; those who supported the Houthis fled on their own to fight alongside them'

– Mohammed, government supporter

“If not for the Houthis, we would still be enjoying peace together in the same village. It is the Houthis who brought battles and hatred to our village.”

Abdulrahman, 64, an uncle to both Mukhtar and Mohammed, believes the war has brought out the worst in society, saying that “one of its ugliest faces is seeing brothers and cousins fight each other”.

“It isn’t easy to see my nephews fight each other, or to see other sons of the village fighting one another,” he told MEE. “This is not the life we should be living. We are one community and must accept each other, even if we hold different beliefs. Fighting only brings the worst consequences.”

Abdulrahman noted that since 4 October, when the Houthis took over the village, new faces among the local youth have come from Houthi-controlled areas, while familiar faces have fled, a shift that deeply saddens him.

“It isn’t easy for people to flee their homes, and it isn’t easy for us to see our relatives absent, unable to meet each other because of political affiliation,” he said.

These two fighters are just one example of "enemy cousins".

Even among senior government officials, some have brothers who have worked with the Houthis for years, reflecting how Yemenis within the same family hold sharply divided loyalties.

Among the high-profile "enemy brothers" frequently cited on social media are the government’s chief of staff, Saghier bin Aziz, whose brother, Hamoud bin Aziz, is a Houthi leader.

Another example is Najib Ghallab, undersecretary of the Ministry of Information for the internationally recognised government, whose brother, Abdel Fattah Ghallab, is also a Houthi leader.

War dragged into homes

Journalist Oday Al-Dukhaini, who covers the fighting in Yemen, said the war has not only divided cousins, it has torn brothers and whole families apart.

“We now see members of the same family standing on opposing front lines, sometimes even taking up arms against their own relatives,” Dukhaini told MEE.

‘Death is closer than school’: Yemen’s children struggle with war trauma
Read More »

“This is deeply painful, because the war has dragged conflict from the political arena directly into people's homes, damaging relationships built on love and kinship over many years.”

Dukhaini emphasised that numerous factors drive individuals to join the fighting, including political and ideological differences, harsh living conditions, and financial need, alongside mobilisation and incitement. Sometimes, a person may not even hold a clear political stance, yet finds themselves aligned with one side due to their circumstances or environment.

“The solution begins with wise elders within the family stepping in to contain the dispute and open the door for dialogue, away from accusations and charges of treason,” Dukhaini added. "Most importantly, everyone must realise that no matter the disagreement, it is never worth turning blood ties into enmity or blood feuds that last for years."

He noted that the war has not only destroyed homes and roads; it has eroded trust within the community.

“Some have begun judging their relatives based on their political stance or the faction they fight for, rather than seeing them as members of their own family and community,” he said.

“Today, we need to mend social relationships above all else; wars may eventually end, but the scars of hatred and estrangement can linger for years.”

Blood ties

Sociologist Hayel Saeed said that while the war might end militarily, its social and psychological impacts could persist for decades if left unaddressed.

“Today, we don't just need a ceasefire; we also need to halt hate speech, incitement and accusations of treason, and restore the values of tolerance, solidarity and coexistence,” Saeed told MEE.

He stressed the importance of reminding parents, social figures, community leaders and elders that their responsibility today goes beyond protecting their families from the physical dangers of war; it also includes safeguarding relationships among their children from disintegration and hostility.

“Your cousin who disagrees with you politically remains your cousin and your relative. A difference of opinion does not cancel out blood ties, nor does it give anyone the right to assault another,” Saeed said.

“Yemen does not only need the war among its people to stop; it needs its people to reconcile with one another and learn how to disagree without turning into enemies."

Taiz, Yemen
